analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Medicare drug coverage gap and repeals private-insurer subsidies and health savings accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in July 2004 to fill Medicare's prescription drug 'donut hole' and roll back private-insurer subsidies, never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Medicare drug law passed in 2003 left seniors a 'coverage gap': after their drug costs passed a limit ($2,250 in the original design), they paid full price until costs were high enough to trigger catastrophic coverage. This bill would have deleted that gap entirely, leaving seniors with small fixed copays ($2 for generic drugs, $5 for others) instead. It also would have repealed three other parts of the 2003 law: a subsidy fund for private Medicare regional plans, a 'premium support' demonstration program, and tax-advantaged health savings accounts. The bill was introduced by Senator Barbara Boxer with Senator Barbara Mikulski, read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and then nothing happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use prescription drugs. Instead of paying 100% of drug costs out of pocket once their spending passed the coverage limit, they would pay a $2 copay for generic drugs and $5 for other drugs, or 5% coinsurance, whichever is larger. This was the period critics called the 'donut hole,' when millions of seniors paid full price for medications. Removing it would shift those costs to Medicare (federal taxpayers).
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare seniors who take prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the initial standard drug coverage limit of $2,250 (adjusted for inflation), the gap in coverage where beneficiaries paid full drug costs, per the CRS summary.
In place of the gap, the bill's text sets cost-sharing at the greater of a $2 copay for generic drugs and $5 for other drugs, or 5% coinsurance, starting with the drug benefit's launch in 2006.
The bill repeals the regional plan stabilization fund, a pool of billions of dollars set aside to guarantee profits for private insurers offering regional Medicare drug plans.

The bill also repeals the premium support demonstration program, a planned test of moving Medicare beneficiaries into private plans, and repeals the health savings accounts created by the 2003 Medicare law.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the richer drug benefit, including the removal of the coverage gap and the new low copays, since no new funding source is specified in the bill. Private insurers offering Medicare Advantage and regional drug plans would lose the stabilization fund subsidy and the premium support demonstration. Banks and financial firms that offered the newly created health savings accounts would lose that product line.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and private Medicare insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill specifies no funding source for the expanded benefit; filling the coverage gap with $2 and $5 copays would substantially increase federal Medicare spending, shifting costs from seniors to taxpayers generally.

Repealing health savings accounts would eliminate a tax-advantaged savings vehicle some beneficiaries had just gained under the 2003 law, a cost to account holders and the financial firms offering them.

Repealing the premium support demonstration would remove a planned test of whether private competition can hold Medicare costs down, an experiment its supporters argued could restrain program spending over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: seniors with serious drug costs would be protected from paying full price in the coverage gap, but the money would come from the federal budget with no new revenue identified, so the public would pay it back in taxes or deficits. The bill bundles the benefit fix with reversals of industry-friendly pieces of the 2003 law (insurer subsidy funds, premium support, health savings accounts), which made it a comprehensive rebuke to the 2003 law rather than a narrow fix, and it never attracted more than two sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 8, 2004, read twice, placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 621, and then sat there untouched until Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with no committee hearing and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the Closing the Coverage Gap Act on July 8, 2004, with Senator Barbara Mikulski as cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 621 on July 9, 2004; no committee was assigned.
After being placed on the calendar, the bill took no further action for the rest of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005; it never received a hearing or a vote.

The bill would have eliminated the Medicare drug coverage gap, repealed the regional plan stabilization fund, the premium support demonstration program, and health savings accounts created by the 2003 Medicare law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private Medicare insurers were better off: the stabilization fund subsidy and the premium support demonstration were not repealed, and the coverage gap that shifted drug costs onto seniors stayed in place. Banks and financial firms kept the health savings accounts created the year before. Seniors in the coverage gap continued to pay full drug costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private Medicare insurers and HSA providers

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate the Medicare drug coverage gap, insurer subsidies, and health savings accounts.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Mikulski
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor listed.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote after it was placed on the calendar; the bill received no floor action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and it never came to a vote, so no roll-call record shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Advantage and regional drug plan insurers
industries.note: The bill repeals the regional plan stabilization fund, a federal subsidy pool guaranteeing insurer revenues, and the premium support demonstration that would steer more beneficiaries into private plans. Insurers kept both because the bill never advanced, while seniors continued to bear the coverage gap's full drug costs.

industries.industry: Banks and financial firms offering health savings accounts
industries.note: The bill repeals the health savings accounts created by the 2003 Medicare law, eliminating a fee-earning, tax-advantaged product line. The accounts survived because the bill never got a vote.

With the coverage gap closed at a flat $2 generic copay, cost to beneficiaries for generics would drop sharply, encouraging generic fill rates. Nothing in the bill changed patent or pricing rules for brand-name drugs.

Closing the coverage gap means drug costs that seniors previously absorbed out of pocket would be covered, increasing demand for brand-name prescriptions. The bill leaves drug prices themselves untouched, so manufacturers gain volume without price pressure.
